events.title: Battle of Vesuvius (Veseris)
events.summary: The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus defeated the Latins and Campanians near Mount Vesuvius on the road to Veseris; when the Roman left wavered, Decius devoted himself and the enemy to the gods of the underworld and charged to his death.
events.detail: Livy preserves the devotio formula, dictated by the pontifex M. Valerius ('Iane, Iuppiter, Mars pater, Quirine, Bellona, Lares, divi Novensiles, di Indigetes...'). Before the battle Torquatus had his own son beheaded for winning a single combat against the Tusculan Geminus Maecius in defiance of orders, the origin of the proverbial 'imperia Manliana'. Livy's set-piece description of the manipular legion (hastati, principes, triarii, rorarii, accensi; 'res ad triarios rediit') at this point is the classic but anachronistic source for the early manipular army. The site is disputed: near Vesuvius, or (Salmon) near Roccamonfina in Aurunca territory, which would better suit the strategic situation.
events.locName: Near the foot of Vesuvius, road to Veseris

sides.strength: two consular armies with Samnite allies (Livy)
sides.losses: heavy on the left; consul Decius killed

battle.significance: Breaks the Latin-Campanian coalition and decides the Latin War.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 405-480
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 206-208
Versnel, 'Two types of Roman devotio', Mnemosyne 29 (1976)
events.debate: Site; historicity of the first Decian devotio (the 295 devotio of his son is better attested and the father's may be a doublet).

events.title: Battle of Trifanum
events.summary: Torquatus caught the regrouped Latins and Campanians at Trifanum between Sinuessa and Minturnae and crushed them; the Latins surrendered and Campanian land (the ager Falernus) was confiscated.
events.detail: The Campanian equites (1,600) who had not revolted were rewarded with citizenship and a payment from the Campanian people; a bronze tablet recorded it in the temple of Castor at Rome.

battle.significance: Final field battle of the Latin War's first phase; ager Falernus annexed.

events.title: Leges Publiliae Philonis
events.summary: The plebeian dictator Q. Publilius Philo carried three laws: plebiscites to bind all citizens, the patrician senators' approval (patrum auctoritas) of centuriate laws to be given in advance, and one censor to be plebeian.
events.detail: The advance auctoritas turned a patrician veto into a formality, and was extended to elections by a lex Maenia of uncertain 3rd-century date. The plebiscite clause appears again in 287; whether the 339 law imposed conditions is debated.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 522-530
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-342

events.title: Battle of the Crimissus
events.summary: Timoleon of Corinth with about 12,000 men surprised a large Carthaginian army crossing the river Crimissus in western Sicily during a thunderstorm and destroyed it, including the 2,500-strong Sacred Band of Carthaginian citizens.
events.detail: The victory confirmed Timoleon's restoration of Greek Syracuse after the Dionysian tyranny and led to a treaty fixing the Halycus river as the Punic boundary. Plutarch and Diodorus date it to 341 or 339. Carthage afterwards relied more heavily on mercenaries rather than citizen troops abroad.
events.locName: River Crimissus, western Sicily (Belice or Freddo?)

sides.losses: 10,000 killed, 15,000 captured including the Sacred Band (Diodorus)

battle.significance: Halycus frontier; Greek revival in Sicily under Timoleon.

scholarship: Talbert, Timoleon and the Revival of Greek Sicily (1974)

events.title: Battles of Pedum and the Astura
events.summary: The consul L. Furius Camillus defeated the last Latin army (Tiburtines, Praenestines, Veliterni, Lanuvini, Antiates) at Pedum while his colleague C. Maenius destroyed the Antiates and Lanuvini at the river Astura; both triumphed and received equestrian statues in the Forum.
events.detail: Camillus then took every Latin town by storm or surrender, ending the League's resistance and opening the way for the settlement of 338.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Furius Camillus, C. Maenius)

battle.significance: End of the Latin League as an independent power.

events.title: The settlement of 338: dissolution of the Latin League
events.summary: Rome dissolved the Latin League and dealt with each community separately: Lanuvium, Aricia, Nomentum and Pedum received full citizenship, Tusculum's was confirmed, Velitrae was punished, Antium became a citizen colony, Tibur and Praeneste remained allies minus land, and Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae and Suessula received citizenship without the vote.
events.detail: The remaining Latins lost conubium, commercium and the right of assembly with one another, keeping these rights only with Rome. This divide-and-rule settlement created the graded system that underpinned Roman Italy: full citizens (cives optimo iure), citizens without suffrage (cives sine suffragio, with local self-government and military obligation), Latin colonies and allies (socii) bound by bilateral treaties to supply troops. It turned Rome from a city-state into a territorial state of perhaps 5,500 km2 and gave it a manpower base no Italian rival could match. Cornell calls it the true beginning of Roman imperialism.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 538-571
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 347-352
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 38-58
events.debate: Whether civitas sine suffragio was a privilege or a burden at this date; the Campanian grant may be of 334 or 318.

events.title: The Rostra adorned with the beaks of Antium's ships
events.summary: The Antiate warships were burned or taken to Rome's dockyards, and their bronze beaks (rostra) were fixed to the speaker's platform in the Comitium, which thereafter took the name Rostra; a column was raised to C. Maenius.
events.detail: Antium, notorious for piracy, was forbidden the sea; a citizen colony was planted there. The Maenian column (columna Maenia) by the Comitium became a landmark where thieves and debtors were tried by the tresviri capitales. Maenius as censor in 318 added balconies (maeniana) over the Forum shops for watching games.

events.title: Citizen colony at Antium
events.summary: Antium received a garrison colony of Roman citizens (colonia maritima) while the Antiates were enrolled as citizens; in 317 they asked Rome for patroni to give them laws.
events.detail: One of the first coastal citizen colonies (with Ostia and later Tarracina 329, Minturnae and Sinuessa 296), small garrisons of c. 300 families guarding the coast and exempt from legionary service.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 70-81

events.title: Vestal Minucia buried alive; first plebeian praetor
events.summary: The Vestal Minucia, suspected for her elegant dress and convicted on a slave's evidence, was buried alive at the Campus Sceleratus by the Colline gate; the same year Q. Publilius Philo became the first plebeian praetor.
events.detail: Vestal executions cluster at moments of military or social crisis (483, 337, 266, 216, 114). Publilius Philo went on to be the first proconsul (326).
events.locName: Campus Sceleratus, by the Porta Collina

events.title: The 'dictator years' of the Varronian fasti
events.summary: The Fasti Capitolini insert four years (333, 324, 309, 301) in which a dictator and master of horse held office without consuls; Livy and the other annalists know nothing of them.
events.detail: They were almost certainly invented by Augustan-era (or late Republican) chronographers, together with the five-year anarchy of the 370s, to reconcile the Roman consular list with Greek synchronisms such as the sack of Rome in 387/386. As a result conventional Varronian dates before 300 are about four years too early relative to 'true' chronology: the Allia of 'Varronian 390' is probably 386. Modern handbooks retain Varronian dates for convenience while noting the problem. In this dataset all dates are Varronian.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 102-104
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 369-370
Drummond, CAH VII.2 (1989) 625-628
events.debate: The fictitious character of the dictator years is generally accepted; how the Varronian system arose is debated.

events.title: Latin colony at Cales
events.summary: After the Ausonian town of Cales was captured, 2,500 colonists were sent there, the first Latin colony founded after 338 and the first planted beyond Latium, controlling the route from Latium into northern Campania.
events.detail: The new-style Latin colony, with Latin rights but founded by Rome alone, became the principal instrument of Roman control: 19 more were founded by 263. Cales became famous for its black-gloss pottery (Calene ware) with relief medallions in the 3rd century.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 55-57

events.title: Alexander of Epirus campaigns in southern Italy
events.summary: Invited by Tarentum against the Lucanians and Messapians, Alexander the Molossian, uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned from Apulia to Bruttium, took Heraclea, Sipontum, Consentia and Terina, and made a treaty of friendship with Rome (332).
events.detail: He fell out with Tarentum, planned to move the Italiote League's meeting place from Heraclea to Thurii, and was killed at Pandosia in 331. His campaign is the first of the great condottiere interventions (Cleonymus, Agathocles, Pyrrhus) that drew Rome into the affairs of Magna Graecia.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 665-690
Purcell, CAH VI2 (1994) ch. 9b

events.title: Tribus Maecia and Scaptia created
events.summary: Two new tribes on land confiscated from Latin cities in 338 brought the total to 29; the people of Acerrae received citizenship without vote.
events.detail: The Scaptia was probably on the old territory disputed between Ardea and Aricia (cf. P. Scaptius, 446).

events.title: Peace treaty with the Gauls
events.summary: Polybius records that after thirteen quiet years the Gauls, seeing Rome's growing power, made a formal peace, which they kept for thirty years until a new movement of Transalpine Gauls.
events.detail: Livy (8.20.2-3) reports that the Senones' threat in 329 proved empty. The treaty, probably with the Senones of the Adriatic coast, freed Rome to concentrate on the Samnites.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 185-186

events.title: The great poisoning trial of 331
events.summary: After many prominent men died of an apparent disease, a slave woman told the curule aedile Q. Fabius Maximus that matrons were brewing poisons; twenty were caught, two patrician women drank their own potions and died, and 170 were ultimately convicted.
events.detail: Livy reports it with reluctance as an act of 'madness' rather than malice; a dictator was named to drive the annual nail as expiation. It was the first trial for veneficium and resembles later mass prosecutions (Bacchanalia 186, poisonings 184 and 180).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 594-602

events.title: Death of Alexander of Epirus at Pandosia
events.summary: Alexander the Molossian, warned by Dodona to beware Pandosia and the Acheron (which he took to mean the places in Epirus), was trapped by Lucanians and Bruttians at the Italian Pandosia and killed crossing the river Acheron by a Lucanian exile.
events.detail: His body was mutilated and parts sent to Consentia; a woman of Consentia ransomed the remains and sent them to his wife Cleopatra (sister of Alexander the Great) and mother Olympias in Epirus.

battle.significance: Ends the first Epirote intervention in Italy.

events.title: Capture of Privernum
events.summary: Privernum, led by Vitruvius Vaccus of Fundi, revolted and was taken; when asked what punishment they deserved, a Privernate envoy replied 'what those deserve who think themselves worthy of liberty', and the Senate granted citizenship. A citizen colony of 300 was sent to Tarracina.
events.detail: Vaccus was executed, Privernum's walls demolished and its senate deported beyond the Tiber. The new tribe Oufentina (318) was formed partly on Privernate land.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Aemilius Mamercinus, C. Plautius Decianus)

events.title: Latin colony at Fregellae
events.summary: Rome planted a Latin colony at Fregellae on the east bank of the Liris, on land the Samnites regarded as theirs, a provocation that helped cause the Second Samnite War.
events.detail: Fregellae was lost to the Samnites in 320, refounded in 313, and became one of the most prosperous Latin colonies until it revolted and was destroyed by the praetor L. Opimius in 125. Excavations have revealed its houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius.
scholarship: Coarelli & Monti (eds.), Fregellae 1 (1998)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 214-216

events.title: Siege of Neapolis and the first prorogation of command
events.summary: Q. Publilius Philo besieged Palaepolis and Neapolis, held by Samnite and Nolan garrisons; his command was extended into 326 'pro consule', the first prorogation of imperium, and the city was betrayed by the Greek leaders Charilaus and Nymphius.
events.detail: Neapolis received a favourable treaty (foedus aequum), supplying ships rather than troops, and remained a Greek city in name and language into the Empire. The prorogation became the key device for extending Roman commands beyond a year. The Samnite reaction to Rome's intervention was the formal start of the Second Samnite War; the Lucanians and Apulians allied with Rome in 326.

battle.significance: First promagistracy; Neapolis becomes a Roman ally.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 628-665
Frederiksen, Campania (1984) 208-212

events.title: Lex Poetelia Papiria: abolition of nexum
events.summary: After the moneylender L. Papirius flogged the debt-bondsman C. Publilius for refusing his advances, public outrage led to a law abolishing nexum: debtors could no longer pledge their persons, and creditors' claims lay against property, not bodies.
events.detail: Livy calls it 'a second beginning of liberty' for the plebs. Varro dates the law to the dictatorship of C. Poetelius (313). Its practical effect was to end debt-bondage as a labour supply, which several scholars (Finley, Hopkins) link to the growing use of chattel slaves captured in the Samnite wars.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 688-700
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 330-333
Finley, Ancient Slavery and Modern Ideology (1980)

events.title: Battle of Imbrinium: Papirius Cursor and Fabius Rullianus
events.summary: While the dictator L. Papirius Cursor was in Rome renewing auspices, his master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus attacked the Samnites at Imbrinium against orders and won; Papirius demanded his execution, and only the pleas of the army, Fabius' father and the people saved him.
events.detail: Livy cites Fabius Pictor here: Fabius burned the spoils so that the dictator could not use them in his triumph. The confrontation dramatises imperium versus popular appeal (provocatio) and the rivalry of two great generals of the Samnite wars.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 700-760

events.title: Alleged Roman embassy to Alexander the Great
events.summary: Arrian reports, citing Aristus and Asclepiades, that a Roman embassy reached Alexander at Babylon in 323 and that he foretold Rome's greatness; Arrian himself doubts it, noting that no Roman writer mentions it.
events.detail: Cleitarchus (per Pliny) also mentioned a Roman embassy. If real, it might relate to complaints about Antiate piracy (Strabo). Most scholars reject it as a later invention, though not all.

events.title: The Caudine Forks
events.summary: Deceived by Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds into believing Luceria was under siege, the consuls T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius Albinus marched through the Caudine pass, found both ends blocked, and surrendered their whole army to Gavius Pontius; the Romans passed under the yoke and gave 600 equites as hostages.
events.detail: Pontius' father Herennius advised either releasing the Romans unharmed or killing them all; his son chose the middle course of humiliation. The consuls swore a sponsio (personal guarantee), not a foedus. Livy claims the Senate repudiated it and handed over Postumius and the officers naked to the Samnites, Postumius kicking the fetial to make Rome's renewed war 'just' (since a Samnite had now struck a Roman), and that Rome won revenge at Luceria in 320. Many scholars (Salmon, Oakley) think the peace was in fact kept until 316, that Rome lost Fregellae and possibly Cales, and that the revenge narrative is patriotic fiction. The defeat drove military reform: Livy (8.8) and others associate the shift to manipular tactics and the scutum with the Samnite wars.
events.locName: Caudine Forks (Valle Caudina, between Arpaia and Montesarchio)

battle.significance: Greatest Roman humiliation of the Samnite wars; five-year peace; spur to Roman military reorganisation and the Via Appia strategy.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 1-160
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 225-232
events.debate: Site of the pass; whether the Senate repudiated the sponsio; historicity of Roman revenge in 320.

events.title: Recapture of Luceria (320)
events.summary: Livy has L. Papirius Cursor besiege and take Luceria, recover the 600 hostages and send 7,000 Samnites under the yoke in revenge for Caudium; Livy himself was unsure whether Papirius or Q. Aulius was in command.
events.detail: Probably a doublet of the genuine capture of Luceria in 314, when a Latin colony was founded. The Fasti Triumphales do record a triumph of Papirius over the Samnites in 319.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 160-200
events.debate: Likely fictional or a doublet of 314.

events.title: Prefects for Capua; tribes Oufentina and Falerna
events.summary: Rome sent praefecti to Capua at the Campanians' request to give them laws, created the tribes Oufentina and Falerna (31 in all), and made alliances with Teanum Apulum and Canusium in Apulia.
events.detail: The praefecti Capuam Cumas, later elected, became the template for prefectures administering communities of cives sine suffragio. The Apulian alliances outflanked Samnium from the east.

events.title: Battle of Lautulae
events.summary: The dictator Q. Fabius Rullianus fought the Samnites at the Lautulae pass between Tarracina and Fundi; his master of horse Q. Aulius Cerretanus was killed, and Diodorus states plainly that the Romans were defeated, while Livy calls it indecisive.
events.detail: The defeat cut the coastal route to Campania and sparked a revolt among the Aurunci and part of the Campanian elite. Rome's response (Via Appia, colonies at Suessa, Pontiae, Interamna) was to secure the corridor permanently.
events.locName: Lautulae pass (Monte S. Biagio, near Terracina)

battle.significance: Samnites break into Latium; Campanian and Auruncan defections.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 290-310
events.debate: Livy's indecisive result vs Diodorus' Roman defeat.

events.title: Destruction of the Ausones
events.summary: The three Ausonian towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia, which had joined the Samnites after Lautulae, were betrayed by young nobles and stormed at night; Livy says the Ausonian people were wiped out ('deleta Ausonum gens').
events.detail: Diodorus reports Roman victory near Tarracina in the same year. A Capuan conspiracy was investigated by the dictator C. Maenius; the Calavii brothers killed themselves. Roman citizen colonies followed at Minturnae and Sinuessa (296).

battle.significance: Annihilation of the Ausones; Liris corridor secured.

events.title: Latin colony at Luceria
events.summary: Captured Luceria received 2,500 Latin colonists, a bastion in northern Apulia behind Samnium, after the Senate debated destroying the town altogether.
events.detail: The far-flung Apulian colony embodied a strategy of encirclement. Luceria remained loyal during Hannibal's war and served as a base.

events.title: Colonies at Suessa Aurunca, Pontiae, Saticula and Interamna
events.summary: Latin colonies were founded at Suessa Aurunca and on the island of Pontiae (313), at Saticula (313) and at Interamna Lirenas (312), consolidating the Liris-Volturnus corridor; Fregellae was refounded.
events.detail: Together with Cales (334), Fregellae (328), Luceria (314) and the Via Appia (312), this ring of colonies isolated Samnium from Campania and Latium.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969)

events.title: Censorship of Appius Claudius Caecus
events.summary: Appius Claudius as censor enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate, distributed the landless (humiles) across all tribes, built the Via Appia and Aqua Appia without senatorial approval, transferred the cult at the Ara Maxima from the gens Potitia to public slaves, and kept office beyond the 18-month limit.
events.detail: The consuls of 311 refused to recognise his Senate list. Legend said the Potitii died out within a year and Appius was later struck blind (hence Caecus). Modern views range from Appius as a 'popular' reformer seeking a clientele among the urban and commercial classes (Mommsen) to a Hellenising aristocrat building state infrastructure for war against Samnium (Humm, Oakley). His secretary Gnaeus Flavius published the legal formulas in 304.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 349-415

events.title: Construction of the Via Appia
events.summary: Appius Claudius built the first great Roman highway, the Via Appia, 132 Roman miles from the Porta Capena to Capua, driving straight across the Alban Hills and the Pontine marshes (the 19-mile 'decennovium' stretch).
events.detail: Initially gravel (glarea); paving with basalt blocks came from 296 onward in sections. The road was a military lifeline to the newly won Campanian lands and the colonies on the Liris, avoiding the Lautulae pass. It was extended to Beneventum (after 268), Venusia and Tarentum, and Brundisium by the 190s. Statius called it 'regina viarum'.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy (1999)

events.title: Construction of the Aqua Appia
events.summary: Rome's first aqueduct, built by Appius Claudius with his colleague C. Plautius (who found the springs, hence 'Venox'), ran 11,190 paces (c. 16.5 km), almost entirely underground, from springs off the Via Praenestina to the Forum Boarium.
events.detail: Only 60 paces near the Porta Capena ran on arches. Frontinus says Plautius resigned after 18 months but Appius remained in office to complete it and so the aqueduct bore his name alone. Its estimated daily discharge was some 73,000 m3 (Frontinus' 1,825 quinariae; conversions vary).
scholarship: Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)

events.title: Duoviri navales and elected military tribunes
events.summary: Plebiscites created two naval officers (duoviri navales) to equip and repair a fleet, and provided for 16 military tribunes for four legions to be elected by the people (lex Atilia Marcia).
events.detail: The duoviri navales attest a small Roman squadron, used in 310 for a raid on Nuceria from Pompeii that went badly, and in 282 off Tarentum. The four-legion army is standard from here on. The same year the guild of tibicines (flute-players), banned from feasting in the temple of Jupiter, went on strike and withdrew to Tibur until tricked back drunk in carts, a famous religious-comic episode (Ovid, Livy).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 382-405

events.title: Battle of the Himeras river (Ecnomus)
events.summary: Hamilcar son of Gisgo defeated Agathocles of Syracuse near Gela at the Himeras river below the hill of Ecnomus; most Sicilian cities defected and Carthage besieged Syracuse.
events.detail: The defeat prompted Agathocles' audacious decision to carry the war to Africa.

battle.significance: Carthage besieges Syracuse; Agathocles invades Africa.

events.title: Etruscan siege of Sutrium
events.summary: With the end of the 40-year truce with Tarquinii, all the Etruscan cities except Arretium attacked the Roman colony at Sutrium; the consul Q. Aemilius Barbula and then Q. Fabius Rullianus defeated them before the walls.
events.detail: The siege opened the second front of the Second Samnite War and set up Fabius' march through the Ciminian forest.

battle.significance: Relief of the gateway colony of Etruria.

events.title: Fabius Rullianus crosses the Ciminian forest
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, after sending his brother, who had been educated at Caere and spoke Etruscan, to scout disguised as a shepherd, led his army through the dense Ciminian forest, until then 'more impassable than the forests of Germany were lately', and ravaged the untouched lands of central Etruria.
events.detail: The Senate, alarmed, sent envoys to forbid the crossing, but they arrived too late. The Camertes Umbri became Roman allies. Perusia, Cortona and Arretium sought a 30-year truce.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 450-500
Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971)

events.title: Battle near Perusia
events.summary: Fabius defeated the Etruscan army near Perusia after crossing the Ciminian hills; Perusia, Cortona and Arretium, the leading cities of northern Etruria, asked for peace and received a 30-year truce.
events.detail: Livy reports another victory near Perusia in 309 (9.40.18-20), perhaps a doublet. Diodorus says Fabius' raid reached Umbria.

battle.significance: Thirty-year truce with the northern Etruscan cities.

events.title: First battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: The Etruscans, having raised an army under a lex sacrata (each man choosing a comrade), fought Rome at Lake Vadimon in the Tiber valley; Livy says it was the bloodiest Etruscan battle yet and broke the 'ancient wealth' of the Etruscans.
events.detail: Livy makes the dictator L. Papirius Cursor commander. The same small lake saw a decisive Roman victory over Etruscans and Boii in 283.
events.locName: Lake Vadimon (Laghetto di Bassano, near Orte)

sides.strength: Etruscan League army under lex sacrata

battle.significance: Breaks Etruscan League resistance; truces follow in 308.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 500-520

events.title: Agathocles invades Africa
events.summary: Blockaded in Syracuse, Agathocles slipped out with 60 ships and 14,000 men, landed on Cape Bon, burned his ships, and carried the war to Carthage's own territory for four years; a total solar eclipse on 15 August 310 BC occurred during the crossing.
events.detail: The eclipse (Diodorus 20.5.5, Justin 22.6) is a fixed point of Hellenistic chronology. Agathocles captured Tunis and dozens of towns, allied with Ophellas of Cyrene (whom he then murdered), and nearly took Carthage, which in panic sacrificed 200 noble children to Baal Hammon (Diodorus). The expedition collapsed in 307 when Agathocles abandoned his army, whose sons he left behind to be killed. It showed Rome that Carthage was vulnerable at home, a lesson applied by Regulus (256) and Scipio (204).
scholarship: Consolo Langher, Agatocle (2000)
Lancel, Carthage: A History (1995)

events.title: Battle of White Tunis
events.summary: Agathocles with about 13,500 men defeated a much larger Carthaginian citizen army under Hanno and Bomilcar near Tunis; Hanno fell and Bomilcar, contemplating a coup, withdrew.
events.detail: Carthage reacted with religious panic, sending offerings to Melqart at Tyre and sacrificing children. Bomilcar attempted a tyranny in 308 and was crucified.

events.title: Hernican revolt and citizenship for Anagnia
events.summary: Anagnia led the Hernici in revolt after Hernican volunteers were captured among Samnites; the consul Q. Marcius Tremulus crushed them, and Anagnia and others received citizenship without vote while the loyal Aletrium, Verulae and Ferentinum kept their autonomy and conubium by choice.
events.detail: Livy notes the loyal towns preferred their own laws to Roman citizenship, an important datum for how civitas sine suffragio was perceived. An equestrian statue of Marcius stood before the temple of Castor.

events.title: Third treaty between Rome and Carthage (the 'Philinus treaty')
events.summary: Livy records a third renewal of the Carthage treaty in 306; the pro-Carthaginian historian Philinus claimed a treaty by which Romans were to keep out of Sicily and Carthaginians out of Italy, which would make Rome's crossing to Messana in 264 a breach.
events.detail: Polybius denies such a treaty existed, saying no copy was in the archives. Modern opinion is split: many accept a 306 treaty with Philinus' spheres-of-influence clause (Cornell, Eckstein); others think Philinus misrepresented it or invented it. The issue bears directly on the 'war guilt' of the First Punic War.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 354-355
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998) 9-16
Serrati, 'Neptune's altars: the treaties between Rome and Carthage', CQ 56 (2006)
events.debate: Existence and content of the Philinus treaty.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman-Rhodian friendship
events.summary: Polybius says that by 167 Rhodes had cooperated with Rome for almost 140 years without a formal alliance, implying informal friendship from c. 306, perhaps tied to trade and anti-piracy interests.
events.detail: Rhodes had just resisted Demetrius Poliorcetes' great siege (305-304). The datum shows Rome's appearance in eastern Mediterranean diplomacy long before the Macedonian wars.

events.title: Battle of Bovianum
events.summary: Both consuls, L. Postumius Megellus and Ti. Minucius Augurinus, invaded Samnium; the Samnite commander Statius Gellius was captured, Bovianum (capital of the Pentri) was taken, and the Samnites sued for peace.
events.detail: Minucius died of wounds (or was replaced by M. Fulvius). Diodorus confirms the capture of Bovianum. Peace with the old treaty renewed followed in 304.

events.title: End of the Second Samnite War
events.summary: The Samnites made peace and the old treaty was renewed; Rome emerged in control of Campania, the Liris valley and northern Apulia, with a girdle of colonies around Samnium.
events.detail: Treaties of alliance followed with the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani (304) and the Vestini (302), extending Roman influence across the central Apennines to the Adriatic.

events.title: Annihilation of the Aequi
events.summary: After the Aequi refused Roman citizenship, the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and P. Sulpicius Saverrio stormed 31 of their towns in 50 days, burning most and nearly exterminating the people.
events.detail: Livy's 'nomen Aequorum prope ad internecionem deletum' is followed by Latin colonies at Alba Fucens (303) and Carseoli (302 or 298) and a new tribe (Aniensis, 299) on their land. A scattered remnant, the Aequiculi, survived around Cliternia.
events.locName: Aequian highlands (upper Anio and Turano valleys)

battle.significance: End of the Aequi as a people.

events.title: Gnaeus Flavius publishes the legal formulas and calendar
events.summary: Cn. Flavius, son of a freedman and secretary to Appius Claudius, published the forms of legal action (legis actiones, the 'ius Flavianum') and posted the calendar of court days in the Forum, ending pontifical monopoly of legal knowledge; elected curule aedile, he dedicated a bronze shrine of Concord in the Graecostasis.
events.detail: Pliny says the shrine's inscription dated it 204 years after the dedication of the Capitoline temple, a key datum for the Capitoline era. Nobles snubbed him: when he visited a sick colleague, young nobles refused to rise, so he had his curule chair brought in. The publication, followed by the first public legal teaching of Ti. Coruncanius (c. 250s), began secular jurisprudence.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 607-650
Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)

events.title: Censorship of Q. Fabius Rullianus: urban tribes and the transvectio
events.summary: The censor Q. Fabius Rullianus confined the 'forensis turba' of freedmen and landless to the four urban tribes, reversing Appius Claudius, and instituted the annual parade of the equites on 15 July (transvectio equitum); for this he earned the cognomen Maximus.
events.detail: Confinement to four of 31 tribes minimised the voting power of the urban poor in tribal assemblies and remained the rule for freedmen (with variations) for the rest of the Republic.

events.title: Expedition of Cleonymus of Sparta
events.summary: Tarentum hired the Spartan prince Cleonymus against the Lucanians and Romans; he took Metapontum and campaigned among the Sallentini, was driven off by Roman forces according to Livy, then sailed up the Adriatic and was defeated by the Patavini near the Brenta.
events.detail: Livy, a Paduan, notes with pride that the prows of Cleonymus' ships still hung in Padua's temple of Juno. Diodorus places him in 303/302. The 'Lacinian treaty' between Rome and Tarentum may date from these years.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60

events.title: Treaty with Tarentum: the Lacinian promontory clause
events.summary: Appian refers to 'ancient treaties' forbidding Roman ships to sail beyond the Lacinian promontory (Capo Colonna near Croton) into the Gulf of Tarentum; Rome's breach of this in 282 provoked the Tarentine attack.
events.detail: The date is unknown: c. 303 (after Cleonymus) is most often proposed, but the 330s (Alexander of Epirus) are possible.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60

events.title: Latin colonies at Sora and Alba Fucens
events.summary: Rome sent 4,000 colonists to Sora on the upper Liris and 6,000 to Alba Fucens beside the Fucine lake in former Aequian land; Carseoli followed (302 per Velleius, 298 per Livy).
events.detail: Alba Fucens, with its 3 km polygonal walls and later Roman forum and basilica (Belgian excavations), became a prison for royal captives: Syphax, Perseus and Bituitus.
